problem: 'Compute Qnet and Wnet. If they differ, the difference is created or destroyed energy, so declare the claim impossible. The machine is PMM-1.' This would make a student reject a perfectly legal engine. A real engine always has Wnet = Qnet because Qnet = Qin − Qout; a claim of Qin = 300 kW with W = 200 kW is normal (100 kW is rejected), not a first-law violation. Only Wnet greater than Qin (energy created) is PMM-1.
fix: 'Compute Qin, Qout and W. Check that W = Qin − Qout. If W is more than Qin, energy is being created and the claim is a PMM-1. If W is less than Qin, the difference is simply heat rejected, which is allowed.'

problem: 'A claim of 125 percent means 25 percent of output is created, not converted' is numerically wrong. With Qin = 100 kJ and Wnet = 125 kJ, the created 25 kJ is 25 percent of the input but only 20 percent of the output (25/125).
fix: 'A claim of 125 percent means that for every 100 kJ of heat supplied, 125 kJ of work comes out; the extra 25 kJ, 25 percent of the heat input, was never converted from heat.'

problem: 'Gives more net work than its net heat input' is imprecise. Net heat input means Qin − Qout, and no cycle can have Wnet greater than that. The PMM-1 claim is that work exceeds the heat supplied, Qin.
fix: 'Form 2: a heat engine in a cycle gives more net work than the heat Qin supplied to it, so η > 1, above 100 percent.'

problem: 'Only a few universities teach PMM-1 as a named topic' is inaccurate. PMM-1 is a standard named topic in most engineering thermodynamics syllabi, usually next to the first-law statement and the Kelvin–Planck statement.
fix: 'Most syllabi treat PMM-1 as a named topic, usually beside the first-law statement.'

problem: The symbol η is used ('so η > 1') before it is defined. The definition only arrives in Section 2.
fix: Define it on first use: 'so its thermal efficiency η = Wnet/Qin is greater than 1, above 100 percent,' then repeat the formal definition in Section 2.
